nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Halt, captain. I am Hanno, customs collector for the port of Ostia. All foreign vessels must declare their cargo. But if you are a trader of good repute, perhaps we can do business.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Captain, the magistrates ask after the olive oil from Athens. Have you secured it?

choices.text: I am still gathering the cargo.
What exactly do you need again?

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: The Athenian olive oil has arrived! The magistrates are pleased. Rome remembers those who serve her well, captain. You will find favorable terms at our markets in the future.

choices.text: Rome is a worthy trading partner.
Where else might I trade in Italia?

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Rome grows, captain, and her people need oil -- for cooking, for their lamps, for their baths. Athenian olive oil is the finest in the Mediterranean. Sail to Athens, buy oil, and deliver it here to Ostia. The Roman magistrates will pay well.

choices.text: I will bring olive oil from Athens.

effects.title: Roman Tribute
effects.text: Hanno, customs collector at Ostia, has asked me to bring Athenian olive oil to Rome. He mentioned Taras and Syracuse as important Greek colonies in southern Italia and Sicilia.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Good. Sail to Athens and buy olive oil -- at least three amphorae. On your way, you might stop at Taras or Syracuse. The Greek colonies there are wealthy and always eager for trade. May Jupiter Optimus Maximus grant you calm seas.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: As you wish. But know that Rome does not forget those who refuse her requests -- nor those who accept them. Choose wisely, captain.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Buy olive oil at Athens -- at least three amphorae of the finest quality. Then deliver it here to Ostia. Simple enough for a captain of your experience.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Athens is east across the sea. Buy olive oil there and return. The magistrates grow impatient, captain.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Rome is still young -- we expelled our last king, Tarquinius Superbus, not many years ago. Now two consuls rule, elected each year, so no one man holds too much power. We are not yet masters of Italia, but mark my words, captain -- Rome will be great. The Etruscans taught us their arts, and we have surpassed the teachers.

choices.text: An ambitious people. What trade do you need?

effects.title: The Young Republic
effects.text: Hanno spoke of Rome's recent transition from monarchy to republic. The last king, Tarquinius Superbus, was expelled, and now two elected consuls govern. The Romans learned much from the Etruscans but consider themselves the superior civilization.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: The Roman Republic, captain. Two consuls elected by the Senate, each serving one year. Below them, praetors, aediles, quaestors -- all elected, all accountable. We also have tribunes of the plebs, who protect the common people from the patricians. It is a system the Greeks would recognize, though we Romans perfect what others merely attempt.

choices.text: Tell me about the early republic.
What work do you have for a trader?

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: The Etruscans ruled Rome before the Republic. They taught us to drain marshes, build arches, and read the will of the gods in the flight of birds -- the augury. Their cities like Veii and Cerveteri are rich with painted tombs showing feasts and games. Braudel wrote that the Mediterranean was shaped by such exchanges between peoples. The Etruscans shaped Rome, and Rome will shape the world.

choices.text: Where else can I trade in Italia?
A proud heritage. I will help Rome grow.

effects.title: Etruscan Legacy
effects.text: Hanno described the Etruscan civilization that preceded Rome -- masters of architecture, augury, and tomb painting. Their influence on Roman culture was profound, from engineering to religious practice.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: South of us, the Greeks have planted colonies across Magna Graecia -- Great Greece, we call it. Taras, founded by Spartan exiles, is rich in wool and pottery. Syracuse in Sicilia rivals Athens herself in wealth and power. These Greek cities trade freely with Rome -- for now.

effects.title: Magna Graecia
effects.text: Hanno described the Greek colonies of southern Italy: Taras (founded by Spartan exiles) and Syracuse in Sicily, both wealthy trading centers. The Romans call this region Magna Graecia -- Great Greece.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Safe travels, captain. Remember -- Rome watches the sea, and those who trade fairly will always find a welcome at Ostia.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: I see you have been trading olive oil, captain. Rome approves. Our baths consume vast quantities, and the lamps of the Eternal City burn through the night. Keep the supply flowing and you will have powerful friends.

choices.text: A steady market is a merchant's dream.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Greek pottery, captain? The Roman nobles collect it eagerly -- those painted scenes of heroes and gods. The Etruscans taught us to appreciate fine craftsmanship. Continue trading it and you will find buyers at every dock in Italia.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Rome hears everything, captain. Our legions march, but our merchants listen.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: The Athenians are expanding their fleet at Piraeus. Nikias of the house of Kephalos pays well for purple dye from Tyre -- the festival of Athena approaches. Greek olive oil is also the finest in the world, though a Roman should not admit that too loudly.

nodes.speaker: Hanno
nodes.text: Egyptian grain shipments have been larger than usual -- the Nile flood was generous. Taharqa at Memphis runs the temple granaries and always needs ships to carry surplus north. Papyrus is also in demand -- our scribes and lawyers consume mountains of it.
